transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
President Trump says White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles is being replaced with Stephen Miller,
who's currently the Deputy Chief of Staff.
Miller is Trump's closest advisor and the architect of his hardline immigration policy.
It's a major shake-up just days after Republicans' historic losses in the midterm elections
and a sign the White House isn't backing down from its agenda, as NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben reports.
Wiles was known to be a savvy political operator.
She saw her job as Trump's top aide to make recommendations, but not necessarily to tell the president no.
Now, Miller, on the other hand, is more like someone who is going to pour rocket fuel on Trump's desires.
He was an aide to Alabama Senator Jeff Sessions, who became Trump's first Attorney General.
And Miller also has a reputation as a policy wonk willing to try new and inventive ways to expand Trump's power.
NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben reporting.
Democrats say they're planning to focus on lowering costs and rooting out corruption when they take control of the House and Senate in January.
NPR's Sam Greenglass has more.
Democrats say first on their legislative agenda is restoring enhanced health subsidies and reversing Medicaid cuts,
reasserting authority over tariffs and trying to end the Iran war.
On these priorities, Democrats are aligned, but they'll need help from some Republicans in the Senate and cooperation from President Trump.
Beyond this early agenda, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's likely the next speaker of the House,
is promising bold dramatic change, though what that looks like is not totally clear.
Some newly elected moderate Democrats are wary of over-promising and under-delivering,
while a new crop of progressives warn against just tinkering around the edges.
A hundred-plus new members will begin arriving in D.C. for orientation this weekend.
Sam Greenglass, NPR News, Washington.
The faculty Senate at Cornell University issued a vote of no confidence against the school's administration this afternoon.
June Young-Han of member station WSKG reports the resolution rebukes school officials over how they handled sexual assault on campus.
The no-confidence measure passed with 75 voting in favor and 50 opposed.
Faculty at Cornell proposed the resolution after a former student, referred to as Jane Doe,
filed a lawsuit saying she was gang-raped at a fraternity house in 2024.
Faculty say the university failed to protect Doe and others from campus sexual violence.
Co-sponsors of the resolution say they've lost faith in the ability of Cornell's administration to handle this issue.
Cornell's President Michael Kotlikoff declined to comment,
but the board of trustees issued a statement saying they are confident in his leadership.
The school appointed former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent investigation.
For NPR News, I'm Jung Yoon Han.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
A new round of bomb threats has forced emergency landings in Europe for the third day this week with fighter jets escorting planes.
Several news outlets have also been targeted.
The Irish government says it doesn't know who's behind the threats,
but it thinks they're likely part of a coordinated effort to cause disruption.
Esme Nicholson has more.
Newsrooms in Ireland, the UK and Bulgaria say that they have received bomb threats,
prompting evacuations that Irish public broadcaster RTE and the Irish Independent newspaper.
The messages sent to RTE and Bulgaria's Nova TV were titled "Message to the West"
and warned that this is the start of a series of attacks on transport across Europe.
The messages come after more than two dozen flights this week were targeted by what have transpired to be hoax bomb threats.
All planes have landed safely and no devices have been found.
Amid concern about a Russian hybrid warfare campaign, aviation security agencies have not ruled out copycat threats or personal grievances.
For NPR News, I'm Esme Nicholson in Berlin.
Former West Virginia governor and longtime Senator Jay Rockefeller died last night at his home in Washington.
He was 89 years old.
Rockefeller, the last member of his family's political dynasty, came from one of the nation's richest families
to spend half a century in public service to one of the poorest states.
He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later
and served two terms and then spent 30 years as a U.S. Senator.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Trump announces Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
Democrats outline January agenda: restoring health subsidies, reversing Medicaid cuts, curbing tariffs, ending Iran war
Cornell University faculty senate passes no-confidence vote against administration over campus sexual assault
Bomb threats against European newsrooms, including Irish broadcaster RTE, prompt evacuations amid flight threats
Former West Virginia governor and senator Jay Rockefeller dies at 89 in Washington
